newsitem.title: USA: Relatives of ValuJet crash victims view fire test.
newsitem.headline: Relatives of ValuJet crash victims view fire test.

text.p: Relatives of ValuJet Flight 592 crash victims Tuesday viewed dramatic videotape of a roaring fire staged to help investigators learn how a blaze started in the cargo compartment of the doomed DC-9 jet.

The video of the test fire was played in the darkened hall where the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) is holding public hearings on the May 11 crash. The DC-9 plunged into the Florida Everglades minutes after take-off from Miami, killing all 110 passengers and crew.

Hearing chairman John Goglia invited relatives to leave the hall before the videotape was played, describing it as "dramatic," but few left their seats. Most watched the video intently, showing little emotion other than one man who wiped his eyes as the lights came on.

"It was a hell of a fire in a very short time. What a tragedy they didn't have fire detection equipment," said Marilyn Chamberlin, mother of pilot Candalyn Kubeck, after watching the video of a fire started and fueled by oxygen canisters similar to those at the heart of the probe.
Two ValuJet ramp agents testified they did not know they were loading hazardous material when they put the oxygen canisters on the plane.
The test fire, conducted Nov. 6 and 7 in Atlantic City, was not meant to recreate the blaze aboard Flight 592 but to help investigators learn more about it, experts said.

SabreTech Corp., the maintenance contractor that handled the generators before they were loaded as cargo on the ill-fated jet, released a letter Tuesday in which it asked the NTSB not to publicly disclose the test results.
The letter said the tests did not fairly mimic condition on the ValuJet plane and would be "highly prejudicial to all of the parties to this investigation".

"This test is a valid and necessary element in our process of discovering all the facts," said Goglia, who chastised SabreTech for its public announcement and threatened to exclude the company as a party to the hearing. "It was never intended to be a re-creation."

In the tests, canisters were loaded into cardboard boxes and stacked in a manner similar to those in the cargo hold, and one canister was tripped. In only about half the tests did the canister produce fire. In tests where it did, the fire took about five to seven minutes to develop, experts said.

The flames burst through the boxes and quickly spread. Loud hissing noises could be heard from the oxygen generators. Temperatures of 3,000 degrees F. were measured. In one test, luggage and a plane tire near the boxes burst into flames.
"It's a crime that the airlines don't regulate themselves," said Chamberlin. "It doesn't cost that much to put fire detection equipment in the hold."
Chamberlin said the test appeared to indicate that if the fire was detected in time, the plane might not have left the ground and those aboard might have lived.

Valujet chairman Lewis Jordan testified for about two hours, answering FAA concerns that ValuJet pilots' paychecks depended on completion of flights, leading to fears they would make decisions that would compromise safety.
"Absolutely not," Jordan said. "I think that is an insult to the industry and to the individual (pilot)."
Jordan vigorously defended ValuJet's safety record, calling statistics that show the carrier had a much higher rate of unscheduled landings than other airlines "misleading."

But asked if the low-cost carrier's rapid growth and outsourcing of maintenance work had stretched ValuJet to the point where it could not detect deficiencies in its operating systems, Jordan conceded that "conceivably was not the best way it could have been done."

Two ValuJet ramp agents who loaded oxygen canisters onto the flight said they had no indication they were loading hazardous material. One said he knew oxygen bottles were not to be put on ValuJet planes.
